meta.title: Who really said "One of the deep secrets of life is that all that is really worth the doing is what we do for others"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Lewis Carroll, in an 1890 thank-you letter to Ellen Terry — though he wrote it as a question. The documented sentence, and how it got tidied.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'One of the deep secrets of life is that all that is really worth the doing is what we do for others'?
meta.ogDescription: It is Carroll — but not from Alice. It comes from a letter to the actress Ellen Terry, 13 November 1890, and he wrote it as a question.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: From a letter Carroll wrote to the actress Ellen Terry on 13 November 1890, thanking her for a kindness. It is not from the Alice books, which is where people usually assume it lives. He also wrote it as a question — the flat declarative version in circulation is a later tidying of his sentence, not a different sentence.

source.heading: The letter

docMeta.dd: Thanking Terry for giving elocution lessons to Isa Bowman, a friend’s child
The Selected Letters of Lewis Carroll, ed. Morton N. Cohen, p. 200 (Pantheon, 1982)

source.excerpt: And so you have found out that secret — one of the deep secrets of Life — that all, that is really worth the doing, is what we do for others? Even as the old adage tells us, “What I spent, that I lost; what I gave, that I had.”
trail: Quote Investigator traced it, and credits Carroll. Its article on this quotation ↗ quotes the 1890 letter in full and concludes: “Lewis Carroll deserves credit for the quotation which he penned in an 1890 letter to Ellen Terry. The phrasing is sometimes simplified when it appears in collections of quotations.” Its citation is The Selected Letters of Lewis Carroll, ed. Morton N. Cohen with Roger Lancelyn Green, letter of 13 November 1890, p. 200 (Pantheon, 1982), marked verified with scans.

Wikiquote reaches the same conclusion. The Lewis Carroll page ↗ lists the popular wording in its sourced Letters section and describes it as a paraphrase of a statement in a thank-you note from Carroll to Ellen Terry, giving the same underlying sentence.

The streamlining is old, not an internet invention. QI records that Langford Reed’s biography The Life of Lewis Carroll — first published in 1932 — already rendered the line in something close to its modern declarative form, in a chapter on the Ellen Terry letters.

This letter is not in the 1898 biography. We searched the full text of Stuart Dodgson Collingwood’s The Life and Letters of Lewis Carroll (1898) ↗, the earliest large collection of Carroll’s correspondence. It does print letters from Carroll to Ellen Terry — one about Shylock and The Merchant of Venice appears at page 182 — but not the November 1890 one, and this sentence appears nowhere in its text. So we cannot show the line in print before 1931.
source.excerptNote: As transcribed by Quote Investigator from the Cohen edition of Carroll’s selected letters. Note the question mark, the capital Life, and the commas around “that is really worth the doing” — all of which the popular version drops.

source.rightsNote: Carroll wrote the sentence in 1890 and died in 1898, but rights follow first publication, and we could not establish when this letter first appeared in print. It is not in Collingwood’s 1898 Life and Letters; the earliest printing we can document is Langford Reed’s biography of 1932, with the standard modern text in Morton N. Cohen’s 1982 edition. Because we cannot place a printing before 1931, we assert no status — credit Carroll as shown, but do not present the text as public domain without checking the edition you are quoting.

author.name: Lewis Carroll
author.heading: About Lewis Carroll
author.bio: Lewis Carroll was the pen name of Charles Lutwidge Dodgson, a mathematics lecturer at Christ Church, Oxford. Under the pseudonym he wrote Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland (1865) and Through the Looking-Glass (1871); under his own name he published on geometry and logic. He was also a prolific letter-writer, and a good deal of what circulates as “Carroll” online comes from that correspondence rather than the Alice books.

cite.sourceCitation: Lewis Carroll to Ellen Terry, 13 November 1890, in The Selected Letters of Lewis Carroll, ed. Morton N. Cohen with Roger Lancelyn Green (New York: Pantheon Books, 1982), 200; as documented by Quote Investigator, “Quote Origin: One of the Deep Secrets of Life Is That All That Is Really Worth the Doing Is What We Do For Others” (25 December 2023). The popular wording is a streamlined form of Carroll’s sentence.

misattribution.heading: What usually goes wrong
misattribution.intro: The name is right. Almost everything else about how this line travels is not.

items.why: It is regularly captioned as coming from the Alice books. It does not appear in Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland or Through the Looking-Glass — we searched both full texts. It comes from private correspondence.

Carroll wrote it as a question put to Ellen Terry — “And so you have found out that secret…?” — not as a maxim. Quotation collections turned the question into a statement, a change QI notes and dates back to at least 1932.

misattribution.truthLine: Carroll wrote it, to Ellen Terry, on 13 November 1890 — as Quote Investigator documents ↗.

context.heading: What Terry had actually done
lead: Carroll had asked Ellen Terry — then the most famous actress in England — whether she could recommend a few elocution teachers for Isa Bowman, the child of a friend. Terry gave the lessons herself. The letter is Carroll, slightly floored, trying to thank her.

That is why the sentence is a question rather than a maxim: he is not handing down wisdom, he is telling her she has just demonstrated something. Read that way the line is warmer and a good deal less pious than the version on the poster.
detailsBody: Isa Bowman was a young actress who played Alice on stage and became a close friend of Carroll’s; she later wrote a memoir of him. Quote Investigator, citing Langford Reed’s biography, records that the favour prompting this letter was elocution coaching Terry gave her, when Carroll had expected only a list of names and addresses.
context.pull: He is not handing down wisdom. He is telling her she has just demonstrated something.
